transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-16 15:00 PDT | Duration: 62m | Attendees: Jordan Price (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Alex Chen (GlacierTech CTO), Priya Rao (GlacierTech ML), Miguel Santos (GlacierTech Infra)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll probably run about an hour, Maya and I will jump into the profiling results and we want to understand your constraints - on prem, vpc, etc.
[00:14] Alex: Yep thanks, Jordan. We're mostly focused on inference latency for multi-turn chat, and cost. We run mixed workloads, some 8k context, sometimes 32k for docs.
[00:28] Maya: Cool, quick agenda — kernel selection differences between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, then CUDA graphs results, KV cache behavior, batching profiles, quantization impact, and finally deployment options for VPC/on-prem.
[00:45] Priya: Sounds good. Also we care about reproducible perf across nodes, and audit / KMS for keys.
[00:54] [00:54] Maya: Right, quick note on the stack we profiled: TRT-LLM with 2.2 conv kernels, FP16 int8 runs, and vLLM latest commit (we pulled from main 09/01) on CUDA 12.3. We used our standard chat workload — 32 requests/s steady, a mix of short/long.
[01:15] Miguel: For on-prem infra, we have A100s, NVLink, and Mellanox 200Gbps. Drivers are 525 series.
[01:27] Jordan: Great, that helps. So first slide — kernel selection. Maya: take it.
[01:31] Maya: Sure. We observed TRT-LLM chooses fused attention kernels on long sequences which reduce kernel launch overhead, while vLLM tends to use smaller modular kernels and runtime decides dynamic tiling. Practically that means TRT-LLM had lower p99 for >8k sequences but vLLM had better single-token latency in some configs.
[01:55] Alex: Could you repeat the p99 comment?
[01:57] Maya: Yeah — p99 for 8k and 32k runs dropped ~25% with TRT-LLM's fused kernels because fewer launches and more contiguous memory ops. But vLLM's approach reducs memory peaks, so it sometimes avoids OOM at the cost of more launches.
[02:16] [02:16] Priya: That matches our testing on smaller models. How about KV cache? we've seen kv cahce thrashing in our internal tests.
[02:25] Maya: Good callout. On KV cache we saw TRT-LLM maintain a contiguous KV layout, which helps NVMe/bus locality, but its cache pipeline is less flexible for partial prefix reuse. vLLM supports sharded KV and more aggressive prefix reuse out of the box. For your multi-session use case that meant lower overall token compute for vLLM when many sessions shared short prefixes.
[02:52] Miguel: Does that affect batching? we need to keep latencies tight for low-SLO queries while still batching for throughput.
[03:02] Maya: Yep — we tested adaptive batching. TRT-LLM benefits from larger contiguous batches due to fused kernels and cudagraphs (we'll show that), so throughput per GPU rises more steeply with batch size. vLLM's fine-grained kernels let it scale better at small batch sizes. So if your SLO requires <70ms tail, vLLM with small batch and prefix cache might meet it more consistently; if you can tolerate higher p50 but need throughput, TRT-LLM + cudagraphs gives better tokens/sec.
[03:35] Jordan: We ran into some transcribe notes, apologies if I mis-say.
[03:40] [03:40] Maya: Now CUDA graphs — this is where TRT-LLM showed big wins. When we capture the forward pass with CUDA graphs for stable sequence lengths, kernel launch overhead drops dramatically and we see near 2-3x improvement in latency for steady-state long prompts. Caveat: cudagraphs require deterministic graph paths; lots of dynamic control flow (e.g., variable-length sampling loops, runtime branching) reduces benefits.
[04:05] Priya: So for chat with varying lengths cudagraphs still help? or only for fixed-length?
[04:10] Maya: You can capture common length buckets and switch graphs per bucket; we implemented a bucketized graph cache. It adds complexity but gives 1.5-2x wins in many mixed workloads.
[04:20] Alex: Any pitfalls with cudagraph replay and KV cache consistency?
[04:23] Maya: Good question. On TRT-LLM we had to ensure KV pointers are re-bound on graph replay. Missing that will replay stale pointers — we included a small rebind step. Also small transcription note — we wrote "cuDAGs" in the notes earlier, meant CUDA graphs.
[04:39] [04:39] Miguel: Drivers and cupti profiling — did you see any issues with CUDA 12.3 + Triton?
[04:45] Maya: We validated on 12.3, 525 drivers — Triton isn't in this bench but TRT-LLM stack integrates with TensorRT libs. We did notice kernel mismatch when driver/CUDA and TensorRT ABI differ; we recommend matching tested stack or using container with pinned libs.
[05:03] Jordan: Moving to quantization — what tradeoffs did you see between INT8 and FP16?
[05:08] Maya: INT8 with calibration can reduce memory bandwidth and improve throughput significantly, but it introduces non-trivial accuracy regressions on some instruction-heavy prompts. For chat, FP16 tends to be safer. TRT-LLM's INT8 kernels were very fast on commodity ops but we saw hallucination amplification on a small set of medical QA prompts. We flagged a few evals.
[05:36] Priya: Did you try per-channel quantization or activation-aware calibrations?
[05:40] Maya: Yes, per-channel and KLD calibration reduced regressions, but cost a lot more calibration time. We included the calibration artifacts in the shared folder (link: https://redwood-internal.s3/ff/glacier/profiles/2026-09-16).
[05:58] [05:58] Jordan: There's a note — we attached the raw perf CSV and flamegraphs in that link.
[06:04] Alex: Nice. Regarding VPC/on-prem — our security team wants KMS + HSM. How does Redwood handle key management for Private deploy?
[06:14] Jordan: For Private we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integration, and audit logs via our Console. For on-prem deployments we can integrate with your Vault/HSM and support SOC2 controls.
[06:25] Miguel: And network egress? we need no callouts to public endpoints from the inference nodes.
[06:30] Maya: We tested an air-gapped flow in our lab; images are pre-baked, control plane can be run in your VPC or we can do an offline handshake. We'll share the ops runbook.
[06:43] [06:43] Priya: Back to perf — can you share kernel timelines? the flamegraphs would help us map hotspots to model ops.
[06:50] Maya: Absolutely — flamegraphs are in the link. High-level: the top hotspots were attention forward and KV memcpy on long sequences. In TRT-LLM the attention op is fused and optimized, in vLLM the memcpy scatter for sharded KV showed up as a bit of overhead.
[07:10] Alex: For our 32k documents, memory is a hard constraint. Did you profile offloading strategies?
[07:17] Maya: We tried NVMe offload on vLLM and it trades latency for capacity; we saw server-side tail spikes when the user suddenly needed a far prefix. TRT-LLM's fused kernels occupy more device memory but with quantization and careful batching we hit 32k for medium models on A100. Offload is helpful but requires anticipating access patterns.
[07:40] [07:40] Miguel: Any recommendations for autoscaling? we want to avoid noisy neighbor effects on shared clusters.
[07:46] Jordan: For Dedicated pools we recommend pinned GPU pools for high-SLO apps or burst capacity with predictable fallback. For on-prem, controlling cgroups and GPU isolation plus per-tenant node pools helps. We can share a config template.
[07:59] Maya: Also something to note: when we enable cudagraphs and kernel fusion, scheduling granularity increases; so autoscaler should consider GPU-level metrics not just pod CPU.
[08:10] [08:10] Priya: One more on evals — can you tie the perf regressions to quality reg checks? we want alerts if speedup causes quality drop.
[08:17] Maya: Yes — Redwood Optimize can be configured to run prompt sets and flag rouge/f1 degradations tied to model/quant profile changes. We'll include sample eval runs.
[08:29] Jordan: Let's recap next steps.
[08:32] Maya: We'll export the CSVs, kernel timelines, and a recommended pilot SOW. We also want your infra spec.
[08:38] Alex: We'll share infra and try to get access for a 1-week pilot.
[08:42] Miguel: I'll coordinate getting access for the bench cluster — might need a short jump host.
[08:47] Jordan: Great. Any final questions?
[08:50] Priya: No, thanks — this was super helpful.
[08:53] Jordan: Thanks all. Meeting adjourned.

Notes / artifacts referenced: perf CSV and flamegraphs (https://redwood-internal.s3/ff/glacier/profiles/2026-09-16), pilot SOW template (link to Redwood Drive: drive.redwood/reports/pilot-sow), ops runbook for air-gapped install (ops/redwood-airgap-runbook.pdf)

Transcript quality notes: Automated transcription with some speaker attribution errors; some technical terms mis-transcribed (cuDAGs vs CUDA graphs, kv cahce).
